newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan enemies of Taleban form military alliance.
newsitem.headline: Afghan enemies of Taleban form military alliance.

text.p: The woes of the new purist Islamic Taleban militia ruling most of Afghanistan deepened on Thursday as their foes signed a military alliance against them.

Already suffering the worst military reverses in their two- year existence, the Taleban were hit by an alliance between Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, ousted government military head Ahmad Shah Masood and Karim Khalilli of the Shia Moslem Hezb-i-Wahadat.

Two weeks after the Taleban took Kabul, the three leaders agreed they would fight the Taleban together unless the militia, born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, stopped attacking Masood.
"Whoever is not ceasing to fight against one of the signatories, the other signatories will jointly fight against them," Dostum spokesman Mohammed Yusuf told reporters.

The pact was signed in Khin Jan, north of the Salang Pass where Masood's renowned guerrillas counterattacked on Tuesday, four days after the Taleban started an assault on his Panjsher valley fortress.

Witnesses said they said seen scores of Taleban casualties being ferried away from the fighting and that the attack had forced the Taleban to break off their bid to battle into the Panjsher to the east of the Salang.
Travellers from the north, from which the Taleban have barred reporters, said Masood's men had staged two ambushes south of the front line on Thursday, killing several Taleban before melting away.

That created severe nervousness among the Taleban at the town of Charikar, a half-hour drive south of the militia's front line headquarters at Jabal-os-Saraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass, Reuter photograher Patrick de Noirmont reported.
He said the Taleban set up anti-aircraft guns on the main street, shops were closed and local people were expecting the worst.
Other travellers said the Taleban had massed about 2,000 men near Charikar, the only sign of major defences between Jabal-os-Saraj and Kabul.
There was no immediate reaction to the alliance from the Taleban in Kabul, but the combined strengths of the three groups that signed it could overwhelm the militia's black-turbanned warriors.
Dostum has probably the best equipped fighting force in Afghanistan and his Uzbeks, descendants of the Mongols of Genghis Khan, are feared as the toughest fighters in a land of tough fighters.

He also has a small air force and at his back are the nations of Central Asia who, along with Russia, have expressed fears publicly of any push by the Taleban and their harsh Islamic Sharia law across their borders.
Dostum had already moved armour and men south of the Salang Tunnel, the main choke point on the highway through the mountains that divide north from south, after the Taleban took Kabul.

Masood, an ethnic Tajik, managed to keep most of his armour and men together in a hasty flight to the Panjsher valley, though he may have difficulty getting them out again after triggering landslides to seal its entrance, military analysts said.

Khallilli, long nervous about the Sunni Moslem Taleban, who are mostly ethnic Pushtuns, controls territory in Bamyan provine to the west of Jabol-os-Saraj, which now appears highly vulnerable to attack from three directions.

In an apparent sign of growing tension on the Taleban side, Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi issued a veiled warning to foreign journalists of reprisals if they continued to make "baseless" reports about Taleban reverses.
